summary.text: For \(n=9\), the primorial is \(223092870\equiv -41\pmod{29^2}\), so its square plus one is divisible by \(29^2=841\) (explicitly, \(49770428644836901=841\cdot59180057841661\)). Hence this term is not squarefree, which already falsifies the conjunction independently of the infinitude claim.

full_proof.text:
Let \(p_0=2,p_1=3,p_2=5,\ldots\) denote the primes in increasing order, and put
\[
P_n=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}p_k.
\]
Thus the sequence in question is
\[
a(n)=P_n^2+1.
\]
(The empty product gives \(a(0)=2\).) We will show that the universal squarefreeness assertion already fails at \(n=9\). This is enough to disprove the stated conjunction, irrespective of whether infinitely many of the terms are prime.

The first nine primes, indexed from \(0\) through \(8\), are
\[
2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23.
\]
Consequently
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_9
 &=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot17\cdot19\cdot23\\
 &=223092870.
\end{aligned}
\]
For example, the multiplication can be organized as
\[
2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11=2310,
\quad 2310\cdot13=30030,
\]
\[
30030\cdot17=510510,
\quad 510510\cdot19=9699690,
\quad 9699690\cdot23=223092870.
\]
Therefore
\[
a(9)=223092870^2+1=49770428644836901.
\]

We now exhibit a nontrivial square divisor of this number. Since \(29^2=841\), divide the primorial by \(841\). One obtains the exact identity
\[
223092870=841\cdot265270+800.
\]
Thus
\[
P_9\equiv800\equiv-41\pmod{841}.
\]
Squaring this congruence and adding one gives
\[
P_9^2+1\equiv(-41)^2+1=1681+1=1682=2\cdot841\equiv0\pmod{841}.
\]
It follows that
\[
29^2=841\mid a(9).
\]
For completeness, the corresponding exact integer factorization at this stage is
\[
49770428644836901
 =841\cdot59180057841661.
\]
Hence the divisibility is not merely a congruential possibility: \(a(9)\) contains the square factor \(29^2\). (Indeed, \(29\) is prime, although primality is more than is needed here.)

An integer is squarefree precisely when no square \(d^2\) with \(d>1\) divides it; equivalently, no prime square divides it. Here \(d=29>1\), and we have just proved that \(d^2\mid a(9)\). Therefore \(a(9)\) is not squarefree.

Now suppose the proposed combined assertion were true:
\[
\bigl(\forall n\in\mathbb N,\ a(n)\text{ is squarefree}\bigr)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\bigl\{n\in\mathbb N:a(n)\text{ is prime}\bigr\}\text{ is infinite}.
\]
Its first conjunct, applied to \(n=9\), would say that \(a(9)\) is squarefree, contradicting the square divisor \(29^2\mid a(9)\). Thus the first conjunct is false. A conjunction is false as soon as one of its conjuncts is false, so no conclusion about the infinitude of prime terms is required. Consequently the conjecture that every term is squarefree and that infinitely many terms are prime is disproved.
